title: Sender Policy Framework (SPF) for Authorizing Use of Domains in Email, Version 1
summary: Email can be forged because existing protocols place no restriction on the MAIL FROM address or the HELO/EHLO domain a host uses. This document defines version 1 of the Sender Policy Framework, which lets domain owners say which hosts may send for them.

plainLanguage.summary: SPF lets a domain owner publish which sending computers may use that domain in the SMTP MAIL FROM or HELO identity. A receiving mail system checks the connecting computer against the domain's DNS record and gets a result that it can use in its local mail policy.

questions: how does sender policy framework work
how does an spf record work
subtitle: How domain owners publish which mail servers may use their domain in SMTP identities.

tldr.problem: Email protocols let a sending host claim a domain in the MAIL FROM or HELO identity without the domain owner's permission. This makes domain forgery possible.
tldr.mechanism: A domain publishes an SPF record in DNS. A receiver compares the SMTP client's IP address and the checked identity against the record using the check_host() algorithm.
tldr.outcome: SPF returns one of seven results, but the RFC does not require a particular action for any result. RFC 7208 obsoletes RFC 4408 and is updated by RFC 7372, RFC 8553, and RFC 8616.

today: RFC 7208 is a Proposed Standard that obsoletes RFC 4408. It is updated by RFC 7372, RFC 8553, and RFC 8616.

sections.title: The Sender Identity SPF Checks
sections.content:
Internet email lets a sending host use a domain name in identities without a protocol-level restriction. SPF lets an Administrative Management Domain (ADMD) authorize hosts to use its domain in the MAIL FROM identity or the HELO identity. MAIL FROM is the envelope sender; HELO is the SMTP client's name from the HELO or EHLO command.

A receiver checks the sending Mail Transfer Agent using the client's IP address and a published SPF record. SPF verifies only the MAIL FROM and HELO identities. The RFC does not recommend checking other identities without explicit approval from the domain publisher.
sections.plainLanguage: SPF checks whether the computer sending a message is allowed to use the domain named in MAIL FROM or HELO. It does not verify every name shown elsewhere in the message.

sections.title: Publishing an SPF Record
sections.content:
An SPF record is one text string in a DNS TXT resource record (type 16) at the domain name it describes. SPF version 1 records MUST use TXT records only. A domain name MUST NOT publish multiple records that would cause one check to select more than one record.

The record begins with v=spf1, followed by terms separated by spaces. A term may be a mechanism with a qualifier: plus means pass, minus means fail, tilde means softfail, and question mark means neutral. A missing qualifier defaults to plus. Several DNS character-strings in one TXT record are joined without adding spaces.

The RFC says a record SHOULD be small enough for the DNS response to fit within 512 octets and gives 450 octets as a guideline for the whole DNS message. Wildcard records are discouraged.
sections.plainLanguage: The record is a DNS TXT value beginning with v=spf1. It lists rules in order, with an optional symbol that says what result to return when a rule matches.

sections.title: How a Receiver Checks a Message
sections.content:
The RFC recommends checking the HELO identity first. If that check gives a conclusive result, the receiver may avoid the more complex MAIL FROM check. If HELO has not been checked or gives no definitive policy result, SPF verifiers MUST check MAIL FROM. When the reverse-path is empty, the MAIL FROM identity uses postmaster at the HELO identity.

The check_host() algorithm retrieves TXT records for the domain and selects records beginning with exactly v=spf1. No matching record gives none; multiple matching records or syntax errors give permerror. Mechanisms are checked from left to right, and the first match determines the result. If nothing matches and there is no redirect modifier, the default is neutral.

Terms that cause DNS queries are limited to 10 in one evaluation; exceeding that limit MUST return permerror. An MX evaluation MUST NOT query more than 10 address records. Implementations SHOULD limit void lookups to two and SHOULD allow at least 20 seconds for evaluation.
sections.plainLanguage: The receiver reads the SPF rules in order and stops when a rule matches. It checks the connecting IP address against the identities and limits DNS lookups so a record cannot trigger unlimited queries.

sections.title: Mechanisms and Modifiers
sections.content:
Mechanisms test whether the connecting IP address is authorized. all always matches; ip4 and ip6 compare the address with a network; a checks address records; and mx checks the addresses of the domain's mail hosts. include runs check_host() for another domain and matches only when that evaluation passes. The RFC says the ptr mechanism SHOULD NOT be published, though implementations MUST support it.

The redirect modifier uses another domain's SPF record when no mechanism matches, unless the record contains all. The exp modifier names a TXT record whose text can explain a fail result. Unknown modifiers MUST be ignored.
sections.plainLanguage: Rules can compare the sender's IP address with a listed network or with addresses found through DNS. A record can also refer to another domain's policy or provide a short explanation for a failure.

sections.title: Macros in SPF Records
sections.content:
Macros let an SPF record insert details from the message or connection into a domain name or explanation. They use forms such as %{s} for the sender, %{d} for the domain being checked, %{i} for the client's IP address, and %{h} for the HELO name. Some letters are limited to explanation text.

Optional transformers can reverse parts or keep a specified number of parts. For example, the RFC says a client IP of 192.0.2.1 expands as 192.0.2.1 with %{i} and as 1.2.0.192 with %{ir}. A percent sign in an invalid form is a syntax error and yields permerror.
sections.plainLanguage: A macro inserts a real sender or connection value into a DNS name or explanation. Transformers can rearrange or select parts of that value.

sections.title: Results and Mail Handling
sections.content:
SPF defines seven results: none, neutral, pass, fail, softfail, temperror, and permerror. A pass authorizes the client to use the checked identity; fail explicitly says it is not authorized. Softfail is a weaker negative statement, while temperror reports a transient error and permerror reports records that could not be interpreted.

The protocol sets no required action for any result. Receivers choose local policy. The RFC says a receiver rejecting a fail during SMTP SHOULD use reply 550 and, if supported, enhanced code 5.7.1. Softfail alone SHOULD NOT cause rejection. Receivers that do not reject SHOULD record the result in Received-SPF or Authentication-Results.

SPF uses the IP address of the last SMTP server. A mailing list or other mediator that resends a message while retaining the original MAIL FROM identity can therefore cause the check to fail.
sections.plainLanguage: SPF reports whether an identity passed, failed, or could not be checked, but each receiver decides what to do. A message resent by a mailing list may fail because SPF checks the server that sent the latest copy.

sections.title: Limits of SPF and Security Risks
sections.content:
Processing limits help prevent a hostile SPF record from causing large numbers of DNS lookups. SPF also verifies only MAIL FROM and HELO, so a message can use a different identity in its From header. A passing SPF result does not verify that other identity.

The check relies on DNS data, which an attacker could spoof to produce an incorrect result. The RFC also warns that macros and explanation strings come from outside the receiver's authority, and DNS queries can reveal information about who is sending mail and where it is going. SPF cannot distinguish individual users who send through the same mail server.
sections.plainLanguage: A passing result covers only the checked SMTP identity, not every identity shown in the message. DNS data, sender-provided text, and some DNS queries also create security or privacy risks.

items.label: None
items.desc: No usable SPF record or identity was found.

items.label: Neutral
items.desc: The domain makes no definite authorization claim.

items.label: Pass
items.desc: The client is authorized for the checked identity.

items.label: Fail
items.desc: The client is explicitly not authorized.

items.label: Softfail
items.desc: The domain weakly indicates the client is not authorized.

items.label: Temperror
items.desc: A temporary error prevented the check.

items.label: Permerror
items.desc: The published record could not be interpreted.
